transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-25 16:00 UTC | Duration ~54m | Attendees: Maya, Diego (Redwood) / Lena, Marcus, Priya (Cinder)

Summary:
  Quick discovery to qualify hosting path (hosted vs dedicated vs private) for Cinder's reranking pipeline. Focus on embedding dimensionality and fanout strategy, vector DB integration constraints, throughput targets, and security requirements.

Topics: embedding dims (768 vs 1536), fanout top-k vs coarse filter, vector DB options, throughput and tail-latency, dedicated capacity, VPC/KMS, pilot next steps.

[00:00] Maya Jensen: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:05] Lena Cho: yes loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:08] Marcus Bell: yep good here.
[00:10] Maya Jensen: great quick intro — i'm Maya, i'm the account lead, diego's with me — he owns infra/benchmarks for serving and he'll be the SE on any pilot. want to start with you, lena, high level what are the key success criteria for this project?
[00:25] Lena Cho: sure, so at a high level we want to improve our product search relevance — specifically rerank on top of lexical results. target is 15-20% uplift in CTR for top-10, and 50–100ms P95 added latency budget for end-to-end search. throughput wise we expect spikes up to 2k qps on peak promos but baseline around 400 qps. security is critical — we need SOC2 + VPC/KMS options and audit logs.
[00:48] Diego Ramos: thanks. quick clarifying Q — is the 2k qps prediction for single-region traffic or multi-region?
[00:54] Marcus Bell: single region, us-east primarily, with EU as secondary.
[00:58] Diego Ramos: ok that makes capacity planning easier.
[01:05] Lena Cho: also curious about cost — we currently run embeddings in-house and use Pinecone for the index, but cost has spiked as dims grew.
[01:14] Maya Jensen: got it — so two dimensions to this: embedding vector size and hosting path. maybe start on embeddings: what model and dim are you using today?
[01:22] Priya Nair: we're running 1536-dim from an open LLM encoder (community model) for product vectors. about 20M vectors total, average doc size has a few chunks so index is around 120M vectors across namespaces.
[01:35] Diego Ramos: 20M * 1536 is a decent index. what's your current average top-k we fanout to from the vector DB?
[01:42] Marcus Bell: currently we retrieve top-200 then re-rank top-20 in a neural reranker. that's proving expensive.
[01:49] Maya Jensen: ok that explains the throughput/cost tension. two common levers: reduce embedding dim (e.g., 768) to cut index size and vector DB cost, or reduce fanout and bias retrieval to recall using_metadata/coarse filters, or host reranking on dedicated infra to make rerank cheaper per-request.
[02:05] Lena Cho: i guess question is impact on accuracy. shrinking to 768 — we've seen small drop in offline eval but not sure about production.
[02:13] Diego Ramos: right, accuracy tradeoffs are dataset-specific. we usually recommend running a small dimensionality sweep — 768 vs 1024 vs 1536 — and then run an A/B on top-N recall metrics. for pilot we can estimate cost/perf: 768 halves index size roughly, also improves throughput for nearest-neighbor lookups.
[02:30] Marcus Bell: can you quantify latency differences? we care about P95.
[02:33] Diego Ramos: ballpark: vector DB lookup times scale roughly with vector size and indexing choice. for approximate indexes (HNSW) P95 lookup at 1536 dim for top-200 on Pinecone-like infra might be 6–12ms per shard, 768 might be 3–7ms. but the big tail comes from network and cold cache — that's why batching and colocating index shards matters.
[02:55] Priya Nair: we saw heavy tail on Pinecone during promotions; P99 spiked to 250ms on some queries which broke our SLO.
[03:02] Maya Jensen: that's where dedicated or private hosting becomes attractive; you can reserve capacity and control placement. also Redwood supports prefix caching and automatic batching for embedding generation and for reranking calls if the reranker is served by Redwood.
[03:14] Lena Cho: how would a hybrid search approach look? we want lexical first then vector, is that supported?
[03:19] Diego Ramos: yes hybrid is common: lexical candidate set (e.g., BM25) then vector fanout. you can also do coarse filtering by metadata to reduce fanout. recommended pattern is top-500 lexical -> vector top-200 -> rerank top-10. but you can tune those numbers. for strict latency budgets we shrink the vector fanout and rely more on the reranker to reorder a small set.
[03:37] Marcus Bell: we tried lexical top-1000 then vector top-300, that crushed our costs. would be helpful if Redwood had suggestions by our cardinality and index sizes.
[03:46] Maya Jensen: Diego will put together a suggested fanout table mapping dims, index size, candidate size, and estimated cost/latency for hosted vs dedicated.
[03:55] Lena Cho: can we talk about the vector DB integration — we use Pinecone today; what's the integration pattern with Redwood? do we need to move indices?
[04:03] Diego Ramos: Redwood supports both patterns: keep vector DB in customer-managed service and call it from Redwood-hosted reranker (we route requests), or host embeddings and the index in Redwood Dedicated (we can host vector indices on managed disks attached to GPU nodes or co-located indexers). For initial pilots, most customers keep Pinecone and we optimize fanout + reranker placement. For scale and cost, Dedicated or Private with co-located indexers gets cheapest and lowest tail.
[04:27] Marcus Bell: if we keep Pinecone, how do you handle auth and network?
[04:31] Maya Jensen: we call Pinecone over the public internet from our hosted runtime; we can set up VPC peering for Dedicated/Private so calls stay inside customer's network. for hosted there are also private link options via marketplace partners in some clouds.
[04:45] Priya Nair: KMS — we need customer-managed keys for embeddings at rest.
[04:48] Diego Ramos: Private deployment supports KMS/HSM integration. Dedicated can include customer-managed keys for model payloads and logs. Hosted supports encryption at rest but not CMK by default unless in a private-hosted arrangement. we'll include that in the security doc.
[04:59] Lena Cho: any comments on quantized embeddings? we heard about 8-bit embeddings to save memory.
[05:04] Diego Ramos: quantized embeddings are promising but add computation at decode time. They reduce disk/memory cost by ~2-4x depending on scheme, but similarity metrics can be affected a bit. good option for archival or very large indexes; for top-tier precision on rerank pipelines we'd test them in an eval.
[05:18] Marcus Bell: ok interesting. what's Redwood's recom for reranker hosting? we currently run a CPU-based cross-encoder for top-20 — it's slow.
[05:26] Diego Ramos: typical pattern: faster candidate generation (lexical+ann) on CPU indexers, then run reranker on GPU-backed inference for cross-encoder. Redwood can host the reranker either in Hosted (pay-per-inference) or on Dedicated GPUs (reserved capacity) — Dedicated reduces per-call cost and stabilizes latency. Private lets you run inside VPC if compliance requires.
[05:42] Lena Cho: cost delta between hosted inference and dedicated?
[05:44] Maya Jensen: hosted is easier to start — pay-as-you-go; for steady throughput (like your 400qps baseline), Dedicated often reduces unit cost materially. we'll share a cost model for your numbers.
[05:54] Marcus Bell: for Dedicated how quick is autoscaling and how do rollouts work if we want a canary?
[05:59] Diego Ramos: Dedicated supports autoscaling with min/max pools and burst capacity. canary deploys and traffic splits are supported at the routing layer — you can pin a model version and route a percentage. if a canary fails, automatic fallback to previous model is supported.
[06:13] Priya Nair: about tracing — we need per-request traceability and token-level cost breakdown for audits.
[06:18] Maya Jensen: Redwood Console provides per-route/model dashboards, tracing hooks, and token-level cost/latency. logs can be exported to your SIEM and we have audit logs for inference calls.
[06:29] Lena Cho: great. i want to probe tail-latency mitigation: you mentioned caching — is prefix/KV cache relevant for embeddings/rerank?
[06:36] Diego Ramos: yes for rerank it's less about KV cache and more about result caching for repeated queries. For embeddings we cache generated vectors for repeated items; for rerank results you can cache top-N results for a short TTL. Also adaptive batching at the inference runtime reduces GPU overhead but needs to be tuned to avoid added latency for singletons.
[06:53] Marcus Bell: how does batching interact with our 50–100ms P95 budget?
[06:58] Diego Ramos: batching can increase average throughput and reduce cost, but naive batching may increase single-request latency. Redwood's runtime uses small-window batching and latency SLOs to keep P95 in bounds; on Dedicated you can configure batch size/flush to meet your SLO.
[07:13] Lena Cho: are there customers who've migrated from Pinecone to Redwood-hosted indices? curious about migration pain.
[07:19] Maya Jensen: yes a couple of retailers moved index hosting to Dedicated with us. migration typically involves snapshot export from Pinecone and re-ingest into the indexer we recommend (FAISS-like or SSD-backed indexes). downtime can be minimal if you run in parallel and cutover traffic.
[07:33] Priya Nair: how do you handle sharding for 20M+ vectors?
[07:36] Diego Ramos: we split by namespace or hash and create multiple index shards. routing is handled by the runtime. you can scale horizontally; for private/dedicated we allocate shards to nodes to minimize cross-node hops.
[07:48] Marcus Bell: do you support multi-VModel (i.e., mixing dims) in the same pipeline? we have some legacy 768 vectors and new 1536.
[07:54] Diego Ramos: yes you can run hybrid pipelines. common approach: keep separate indices and either coalesce results by score normalization or re-embed legacy content on a target dim. for short term we can do hybrid retrieval and then normalize scores before reranking.
[08:08] Lena Cho: i want to discuss pilot scope — what would a minimal pilot look like to validate uplift and latency?
[08:14] Maya Jensen: typical pilot: ingest a slice of your catalog (e.g., 1M vectors), run side-by-side traffic for small % of requests or a replay of logs, test 768 vs 1536 sweep, and measure P95/P99 and cost. Redwood provides the runtime and helper scripts for ingestion and scoring.
[08:30] Marcus Bell: for side-by-side we prefer a replay approach to avoid customer-facing variance.
[08:34] Diego Ramos: replay is recommended — provide a day's worth of queries and we'll run deterministic eval with your index and our suggested configs.
[08:41] Priya Nair: what's the timeline for pilot setup?
[08:44] Maya Jensen: we can spin up a pilot environment within 2–3 business days once contracts are signed and we get access keys/logs.
[08:51] Lena Cho: are there any infra blockers for us to run a quick pilot — e g, data residency?
[08:56] Diego Ramos: for hosted, data will transit our control plane; if you need data never leave your VPC then Private deployment is required. Also, some countries need in-region storage — we support regional hosting where available.
[09:09] Marcus Bell: security/commonly asked Q — do you support SAML SSO and RBAC for team access?
[09:14] Maya Jensen: yes SAML, SSO integrations, org-level RBAC and audit logs are supported. enterprise packages include dedicated support for compliance.
[09:23] Lena Cho: earlier you mentioned approximate numbers for lookup latencies — can we get more concrete numbers tailored to our 20M x 1536 index?
[09:31] Diego Ramos: i'll prepare a quick estimate: for your index on a 4-shard HNSW layout, expected P95 lookup per shard ~8–12ms at 1536, aggregated lookup maybe 12–25ms depending on parallelism and network. then reranker GPU inference P95 depends on model — a small cross-encoder on GPU can be 12–30ms per item if batch optimized. we'll put these in the benchmark note.
[09:55] Marcus Bell: about estimates — do you include networking and serialization overheads?
[09:59] Diego Ramos: yes we try to include network RTT, serialization, and any cold-cache penalty in our conservative estimates.
[10:05] Lena Cho: curious on pricing model for Dedicated — is it flat for reserved nodes or usage-based?
[10:09] Maya Jensen: Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly/annual commit; there are options for burst capacity. hosted is usage-based per token/inference. we'll include numbers based on your QPS and estimated token volumes.
[10:21] Priya Nair: do you support on-prem private deployments for air-gapped setups?
[10:25] Diego Ramos: yes, we have an on-prem package for regulated workloads; that typically takes longer to provision and requires some integration work.
[10:34] Lena Cho: ok what deliverables should we expect from Redwood before next call?
[10:38] Maya Jensen: we'll send: security whitepaper, hosted vs dedicated cost comparison for your numbers, a short benchmark note on fanout dims, and a pilot proposal with steps and timeline.
[10:50] Marcus Bell: that sounds good.
[10:52] Diego Ramos: a few technical clarifications we'll need: sample queries (replay), current index stats per namespace, and access to any metric dashboards for the last 7 days to model spikes.
[11:03] Priya Nair: i'll get the logs — maybe a redacted trace for privacy.
[11:06] Lena Cho: timeline — can we aim to start pilot mid-March?
[11:09] Maya Jensen: that's feasible assuming contract and infra access; we'll try for March 15th start.
[11:15] Marcus Bell: what about fallback policies if reranker service degraded?
[11:18] Diego Ramos: Redwood routing supports automatic fallback to a cheaper model or lexical-only path; you can configure thresholds for error rates and latency to trigger fallback.
[11:28] Lena Cho: competition — we've evaluated Milvus and Pinecone; curious if Redwood has benchmarked against them.
[11:33] Maya Jensen: we do internal benchmarks across common indexers — we'll share representative results but recommend you run your own replay since workload nuances matter.
[11:41] Marcus Bell: final Q — data retention and log access for audits?
[11:45] Maya Jensen: logs can be retained per your policy and exported. enterprise agreements add longer retention and access controls.
[11:52] Priya Nair: ok thanks — that's helpful.
[11:55] Maya Jensen: great recap: Maya to send pricing/security, Diego to send bench note and fanout recommendations, Priya and Marcus to supply logs and index stats. We'll schedule follow up after you review materials.
[12:06] Lena Cho: thanks everyone.
[12:08] Marcus Bell: thanks, bye.
[12:10] Diego Ramos: thanks, bye.

Notes about transcript quality: auto transcription had trouble with some proper nouns (model names) and overlapped speech near the end; timestamps are approximate.
